name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,888

clue.text: Difficult crossword arrived? Bugger, you might say

blocks.note: the Listener is the famously hard weekly barred-grid puzzle in the Times, the one solvers name when they mean difficult
a train that has arrived is in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Difficult crossword' sits where a definition usually sits and is the wordplay instead. The bugger is the one who plants the bug, not an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugger → LISTENER-IN: someone who bugs a room does it to eavesdrop, and a listener-in is precisely that person, secretly on the line.

clue.text: Five Turkish and British commanders in Rover

blocks.note: V is five in Roman numerals
an aga was a commander in the Ottoman army, a Turkish military title
James Bond's rank in the Royal Navy is Commander, which is how his letters are asked for

explanation.walkthrough: The Rover is a car on the surface, and 'commanders' does double duty: one is an Ottoman title, the other a naval rank held by a fictional spy.
explanation.definitionFit: Rover → VAGABOND: a rover is someone who wanders with no fixed home, and that homeless wandering is what the noun names.

clue.text: Reversible instrument

indicators.note: A reversible garment can be worn either way out and is the same garment, so the letters must work from either end.

blocks.note: not a violin: in law an instrument is a formal written document that does something, such as transferring a house

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and one job each: the first says what shape the answer has to have, the second says what it is. The legal sense is the only one that fits.
explanation.definitionFit: instrument → DEED: lawyers call any formal document an instrument, and the deed is the one that hands ownership of property from one party to another.

clue.text: Miraculous nun is at God's disposal

definitions.note: The answer is an -ing form used as a plain adjective, so an adjective without that ending defines it perfectly well.

indicators.note: Getting rid of something means throwing it out, and what is thrown out lands in whatever order it happens to fall.

blocks.note: ten letters handed over whole, to be put back in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a piece of piety and the letters are the point: a convent, a saint and a miracle are all there to disguise ten characters waiting to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Miraculous → ASTOUNDING: both describe something so far outside the ordinary that it stops you dead, one by wonder and one by disbelief.

clue.text: Country walk with first half climbing attractive rock

indicators.note: Half of a six-letter word is three letters, and 'first' says it is the front three that are wanted.
A down entry climbs from the bottom of the grid to the top, so the letters it points at are read upwards, in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a ramble is a walk in the country, and the word splits down the middle so that its front three can be turned

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one hillwalking scene, and only the last two words are the definition — everything in front of them is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: attractive rock → MARBLE: the stone is quarried for its looks, which is why sculptors and architects choose it, so 'attractive' is doing real work.

clue.text: Fierce wife is lady every so often

indicators.note: Something done every so often happens at intervals rather than continuously, so letters are picked at every other position.

blocks.note: W is the standing abbreviation for a wife
the first, third and fifth letters of these two words, counted straight through

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wife is lady' is gallantry on the surface and raw material underneath: the first word is an abbreviation, the other two are only a source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fierce → WILD: a wild animal is an untamed and dangerous one, so the definition takes the savage sense rather than the uncultivated-countryside one.

clue.text: Bright church strangely frightening

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation printed against a church on an Ordnance Survey map
something strange and frightening is eery, the older spelling of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' begs to be an instruction to shuffle. It is nothing of the kind: it joins the word after it to make one plain synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Bright → CHEERY: of a person or a room, bright means lively and good-humoured rather than well-lit, and that is the sense wanted.

clue.text: Senior clergyman intimate with very becoming maidens

indicators.note: One thing becoming another has changed into it, so the letter named first is not added but replaced by the letter named second.

blocks.note: an intimate detail is a private one
V is the everyday shorthand for very, as in 'v good'
in cricket a maiden is an over off which no runs are scored, and the scorebook marks it M; the plural belongs to the surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Becoming maidens' reads as a compliment and is an instruction. The clergyman is an archbishop — Canterbury holds the title Primate of All England.
explanation.definitionFit: Senior clergyman → PRIMATE: a primate is the chief bishop of a national church, so the definition names the office rather than any one holder.

clue.text: Young animal had to enter cocoon

blocks.note: a pup is a young dog or seal
someone who had lunch ate it — the past tense of the meal, not of owning

explanation.walkthrough: Two everyday words laid end to end with no indicator anywhere to say so, which is what makes the join hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: enter cocoon → PUPATE: a caterpillar pupates when it seals itself up to transform, and spinning a cocoon around itself is how many species do it.

clue.text: European sleeps on Channel Tunnel line, going back

indicators.note: In an across clue one thing sitting on another comes after it, so the sleeper follows the railway rather than leading it.
An across entry that goes back runs right to left, so the assembly is written out the other way round.

blocks.note: HS1 is High Speed 1, the rail line from London to the tunnel, and its 1 does duty as the Roman numeral
someone who sleeps briefly naps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleeps on' sounds like a bad night on a train, which is the disguise. The line wanted is not the Eurostar service but the track it runs on.
explanation.definitionFit: European → SPANISH: an adjective defined by the wider class it belongs to, since anything Spanish is European — definition by example.

clue.text: Scotch added on drinks dad and I had

indicators.note: To drink something is to take it right inside you, so the phrase beside it swallows the letters that follow.

blocks.note: to put one thing to another is to add it on, and the phrase opens up between its two words
pa is the familiar word for a father
the clue's own word, taken at face value
had shrinks to the 'd of I'd, the same contraction spoken aloud every day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' is a verb here rather than a whisky, which is what the drinking family is there to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotch → PUT PAID TO: to scotch a rumour is to finish it off for good, which is exactly what putting paid to something does.

clue.text: Harry deprived of king's insignia

indicators.note: Being deprived of something means it has been taken away from you, so the letter named next never appears.

blocks.note: to harry someone is to nag and pester them — the verb English borrowed from the black-and-white animal that digs setts
R is rex, Latin for king, the letter a monarch signs after their name

explanation.walkthrough: Harry is a name on the surface — a prince, even, given the king standing next to him — and a plain verb underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: insignia → BADGE: insignia are the emblems worn to show rank or membership, and a badge is one such emblem pinned or sewn on.

clue.text: Part of bolt on doorframe painted round

indicators.note: Part of something is a piece cut out of it, so only a stretch of the words that follow is wanted, not their meaning.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters straddle these three words, beginning inside the first

explanation.walkthrough: The ironmongery is a decoy: nothing is bolted to anything, and the words are only a place for five letters to sit in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: painted round → TONDO: a tondo is a picture made in a circular format, so the definition names the work by the shape that defines the form.

clue.text: For real crime, Capone cleared out bank

indicators.note: A room cleared out has had its contents removed, so the word keeps the two letters at its ends and loses the middle.

blocks.note: a sin is a wrongdoing — the church's word for a crime
the first and last letters of the gangster's name, with everything between gone
to bank on someone is to rely on them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' comes last and looks like the definition, which is where the Chicago money surface is pushing. It is a verb, and the definition is the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: For real → SINCERELY: 'for real' is the colloquial way of saying something is genuinely meant, which is how anything done sincerely is done.

clue.text: Think a lot of groups ran past?

blocks.note: things that belong together form a set
to tear off somewhere is to run at speed
walking past someone is walking by them

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay's three words are not the answer's three words: the enumeration moves the first join one letter along, and that shift is what makes the phrase hard to see coming.
explanation.definitionFit: Think a lot of → SET STORE BY: to set store by something is to rate it highly, an idiom that only ever appears whole.

clue.text: Editor's lead article in fact without substance

indicators.note: The lead is the front position, so the word beside it gives up the single letter that leads it off.

blocks.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken
the definite article, spelled out in full rather than abbreviated
both phrases introduce the truth behind an appearance

explanation.walkthrough: An editor is usually ED in a crossword, which is one letter too many here, and the newsroom surface exists to make you reach for it.
explanation.definitionFit: without substance → ETHEREALLY: something done ethereally is done with an airy, insubstantial lightness, which is what having no substance describes.

clue.text: Heroic term interchangeable with "Centre of roundabout west of Paris"

definitions.text: Heroic term interchangeable with "Centre of roundabout west of Paris"

indicators.note: Two things that are interchangeable can swap places freely, and so can these letters.
The centre of a word is what sits at its middle, equally far from either end — here two letters out of ten.
West is the left-hand end of an across entry, so it points at the letter a word starts with.

blocks.note: ten letters handed over whole, to be rearranged around the three that follow
the middle pair of a ten-letter word
only the opening letter of the word is taken, the one standing at its western end

explanation.walkthrough: Read once it is a description of a monument; read again the same words are all letters, two of them prised out of the description itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the name means 'arch of triumph', and the monument stands at the hub of a huge roundabout in western Paris.

clue.text: Strong cold wind around island impaired hearing

indicators.note: What goes around something encircles it, so the word beside it opens up and takes the single letter into its middle.

blocks.note: the mistral is the fierce cold wind that funnels down the Rhône valley into southern France
I is how an island is labelled on a map

explanation.walkthrough: 'Impaired hearing' reads as deafness. The hearing is a court's, not an ear's, and the wind has blown in from a weather forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: impaired hearing → MISTRIAL: a trial is a court hearing, and a mistrial is one invalidated by an error in the proceedings — a hearing gone wrong.

clue.text: States positively upset, losing American accent

indicators.note: Something upset has been tipped over, and in a down entry that means reading the letters from the bottom of the grid to the top.
To lose something is to be left without it, so the letter named next never joins the others.

blocks.note: to state something positively is to assert it
A is the standard abbreviation for American, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'American accent' is the trap: the two words look like one phrase and belong to opposite halves of the clue, one a letter to drop and one the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: accent → STRESS: in speech the accent falls on a syllable, and that emphasis is its stress — the pronunciation sense, not the regional one.

clue.text: British label on pants giving one away in German's house

indicators.note: In an across clue a thing on another comes after it, so the label lands behind what it is attached to.
To give something away is to part with it for nothing, so the letter named here is handed over and never appears.

blocks.note: B is the standing abbreviation for British
pants are undies, and the word arrives one letter short
one is the Roman numeral I, and this is the letter that goes
the label sewn into a garment is its tag

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a laundry complaint. 'House' is the parliamentary sense — the House of Commons sort — and the German one sits in Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: German's house → BUNDESTAG: the Bundestag is Germany's elected parliamentary chamber, so 'house' means a legislative body rather than a building.

clue.text: Too near

definitions.note: The first sense is the older adverb, now nearly always written with a final S; the setter is using the bare form the dictionaries still list.

blocks.note: the sense 'in addition, over and above what has already been said'
the everyday positional sense: at the side of something, right next to it

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no wordplay at all, which is why the clue looks unfinished: one is an archaic adverb, the other the preposition everybody knows.
explanation.definitionFit: near → BESIDE is standing at the side of something; Too → BESIDE is the older 'in addition' sense, the one that usually carries an S today.

clue.text: Reprimand headless chicken?

indicators.note: A headless word has lost the letter at its front, which in a down entry is the one at the top.

blocks.note: calling somebody chicken says they are fearful, and the word then loses its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: A headless chicken is a proverbial picture of panic, which is exactly what the setter wants you to see instead of an instruction to behead a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Reprimand → EARFUL: giving somebody an earful is subjecting them to a loud telling-off, so the noun names the scolding itself.

clue.text: Fish squirted water from mouths across river

indicators.note: A bridge across a river spans it from bank to bank, so the word beside it is laid over the letter and takes it inside.

blocks.note: mouths that squirted water spat, in the past tense the clue is using
R is the map's abbreviation for a river

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish squirted water' reads as one statement about a fountain. The definition is the first word by itself and everything after it is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish → SPRAT: a sprat is a small sea fish of the herring family, so the general word defines it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Separate intro for song on record

indicators.note: An intro is the opening of a piece of music, so the word after it gives up its first letter and nothing more.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word, taken on its own
the hottest day on record is the hottest one going

explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like it wants one of the crossword's discs — LP, EP, CD are all four letters or fewer. It belongs to a phrase instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Separate → SEVER: to sever is to cut something apart, the abrupt end of the same idea, and both work as transitive verbs.

clue.text: End of manoeuvres in tank covering great area

indicators.note: The end of a word is the letter you reach last, and only that one is taken.
A piece that goes in something drops inside it, splitting the other word apart rather than joining it at either end.

blocks.note: a vat is the great tub a brewery keeps its liquid in
the final letter of the word, taken on its own

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last three words, which read as part of the description of the tank — that is what makes the clue look like one military sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: covering great area → VAST: something vast is immense in extent, so a phrase about how much ground it covers stands in for the adjective.

clue.text: News in the paper concerning Republican in the soup

indicators.note: Whatever is in the soup is down inside it, so the letter named beside this phrase lands in the middle of the word for it.

blocks.note: RE heads a memo about something — the crossword's usual word for concerning
potage is a thick soup, straight off a French menu
R is the standard abbreviation for a Republican in American politics

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, being in the soup means being in trouble, which is where the politician appears to be. The soup here is French and on the menu.
explanation.definitionFit: News in the paper → REPORTAGE: reportage is journalism taken as a body of reported material, rather than any single article or bulletin.

clue.text: Lick a bit of expensive cappuccino up

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a piece broken off its front, so only the opening letters of what follows are wanted.
A down entry read upwards runs from the bottom of the grid to the top, so the letters go in the other order.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word, and no more of it
a cap is what a coffee bar calls a cappuccino, the front of the word standing in for the whole

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lick' at the head of the clue looks like a verb, someone stealing a mouthful of froth, and it is a noun about speed — the joke the whole surface rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: Lick → PACE: 'at a fair lick' is British for at a fair speed, so the slang noun and the plain one name the same thing.

clue.text: Offer to cover tracks reflected trouble

indicators.note: To cover something is to lie over it and hide it, so the word beside it closes around the other one.
A reflection shows you the same thing the other way round, so the assembly is read from its far end.

blocks.note: an offer at auction is a bid, and it opens up to take another word inside
the tracks worn into a muddy lane are ruts

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover your tracks' is one idiom on the surface and two separate instructions underneath: one word to do the wrapping, another to be wrapped.
explanation.definitionFit: trouble → DISTURB: to trouble somebody is to disturb them — 'sorry to trouble you' and 'sorry to disturb you' are the same apology.

clue.text: French drink tea with delight, mostly

indicators.note: Mostly means nearly all of it, so the word beside it turns up with its final letter missing.

blocks.note: cha is the British slang word for tea, taken from the Chinese name for it
delight is bliss, arriving one letter short

explanation.walkthrough: 'French drink tea' reads as a single sentence about national habits, and the definition stops after the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: French drink → CHABLIS: Chablis is a dry white wine from the northern edge of Burgundy, so the general phrase points at one instance of it.
